newsitem.title: USA: Hot manufacturing sector cools as orders dip.
newsitem.headline: Hot manufacturing sector cools as orders dip.

text.p: The nation's hot manufacturing sector showed signs of cooling in March, according to a government report on Tuesday showing the biggest drop in factory orders since last summer.

Orders received by factories fell 1.6 percent in March to a seasonally adjusted $319.2 billion after rising by a smaller-than-previously estimated 0.4 percent in February, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday.
The broad-based decline, which had been expected, was the biggest drop in demand for manufactured goods since last August and the first retracement this year.
Several economists agreed that the manufacturing sector and the general economy were slowing down somewhat from their active pace of the first quarter.

"I think the combination of all recent data is pointing in the same direction and that is that the economy is definitely slowing in the second quarter," said economist Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette in New York.
"The question is how slow," she added.

Despite the March decline, factory orders so far this year are still running 5.7 percent ahead of their 1996 pace. And the industrial sector chugged along at a busy 84.1 percent of its capacity in March.
"I think we've seen the best of the manufacturing growth rate," said economist Daryl Delano of Cahners Economics in Newton, Mass.

"(The report) certainly does give us further evidence that although the manufacturing sector is still healthy, when you compare it to six months or a year ago, it has lost some of its momentum as we move into the second quarter," said Delano.

Economist Robert Dederick of Northern Trust Co. in Chicago downplayed the significance of the order decline, noting that manufacturing had led the economy to an impressive 5.6 percent growth rate in the first quarter.
"When you put it in perspective, you find that orders are actually still pretty impressive in March," said Dederick.

Separately, a survey of the National Association of Purchasing Management predicted that the economy will slow temporarily from the first quarter's torrid pace but pick up steam again in the second half of the year. NAPM members buy raw and processed materials for manufacturers.
Meanwhile, Conference Board Chief Economist Gail Fosler predicted strong economic growth of about 3.25 percent to 3.5 percent for 1997. The economy grew 2.4 percent last year.
Economists widely believe that Federal Reserve policymakers believe the economy's growth rate should stay within the 2-percent-to-2.5-percent growth rate they have projected for the year.
The central bank already lifted short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point in March in an effort to put the brakes on an economy it saw as overactive and potentially inflationary.
Economists believe that, even with the more leisurely pace of manufacturing activity suggested by the factory orders report, the Fed will raise rates again, possibly on May 20.

Factory inventories rose 0.2 percent to $442.7 billion in March, the eighth rise in the last nine months, while order backlogs registered their first drop since last August, declining 0.4 percent to $520.1 billion, the department said.

Shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, slipped 0.1 percent to $321.2 billion in March, but were still running 6.7 percent ahead of last year's pace, it said.
Orders for long-lasting durable goods, items that account for about half of total factory business, fell 3 percent in March, while orders for non-durable goods slid 0.3 percent.
Among the largest declines in March was a drop in orders for transportation equipment, which fell 4.6 percent.
Shipments of motor vehicles and parts fell 1.8 percent, after a 1.9 percent drop in February. In the automobile industry, shipments correspond to orders.
Excluding transportation, factory orders fell 1.2 percent in March after rising in February by 1.5 percent.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, declined by 4 percent in March, but were still running slightly ahead of last year's pace.
Defence contractors' orders, which are subject to wide monthly swings, dropped by 13.7 percent in March. Excluding defence industries, factory orders were down 1.4 percent.
Orders for industrial machinery fell 1 percent, bookings for electronic and electrical equipment fell 4.9 percent and orders for primary metals rose 0.3 percent.
